# Assignment of Copyright

## When to use this

Use this whenever an individual has created something the Kingdom intends to own,
register, or enforce — the Charter text, the seal and any artwork, liturgy,
teaching materials, hymns and recordings, photographs, website copy, curricula,
the contents of this system, a logo drawn by a member on a Saturday afternoon.

Take one from every author, and take it early. The Founder should execute one for
every work they personally created that the Kingdom intends to enforce; so should
every volunteer, contractor, designer, photographer, and employee whose work the
Kingdom is relying on. There is no exception for the founder of the institution,
and no exception for a gift freely given: what the Kingdom does not hold in a
signed writing, the Kingdom does not own.

The consequence is not theoretical. It surfaces on the standing question, midway
through an enforcement matter the Kingdom was otherwise going to win, when the
other side asks who the copyright owner is and the answer turns out to be a
volunteer who moved to Ohio in 2019.

Use it for copyright only. A trademark assignment is a different instrument and
must carry the goodwill of the business with the mark or it is void. A patent
assignment is different again. And this form transfers rights in a *work*; it is
not a transfer of the physical object, which passes separately and carries no
copyright with it.

## Before you send

- [ ] **The work is identified precisely enough that a stranger could tell what is
      being assigned.** Title, medium, date of creation, date and place of first
      publication if published, and where the file or original sits. Schedule A
      does this and it is the part most often filled in carelessly.
- [ ] **The true author is the person signing.** Where two or more people
      contributed copyrightable expression to a single work, they are joint
      authors and each must sign. Where the work incorporates someone else's
      material — a stock photograph, a font, a sampled recording, a chunk of code
      under a licence — that material is not the author's to assign and the
      instrument must say so.
- [ ] **The ownership history is honest.** If the work was made for another
      employer within the scope of that employment, it may already belong to them
      and the author cannot give it away. Ask the question before the signature,
      not after.
- [ ] **Consideration is real, stated, and actually paid or given.** A dollar
      figure that is never paid is a fact an adversary will find.
- [ ] **The grantee is named exactly as the Kingdom's governing instrument names
      the entity that is to hold the work,** and someone has confirmed that the
      entity as constituted can take and hold title. A grant to a name
      corresponding to no legal person is a defect that surfaces on the standing
      question, which is the worst possible moment.
- [ ] **Any work of visual art has the § 106A waiver considered** — the seal, a
      painting, a sculpture, a limited-edition photographic print. The waiver must
      specifically identify the work and the uses to which it applies.
- [ ] **Nothing in the draft purports to waive the author's termination right**
      under 17 U.S.C. § 203. It cannot be waived, and a clause attempting it
      signals that the drafter did not know the statute.
- [ ] **A notary is arranged.** Notarisation is not required for validity and is
      taken anyway, because the argument the Kingdom will actually face is a
      denial of signature.
- [ ] **The work is recorded in the Intellectual Property Portfolio** with the
      executed assignment attached, and a record opened in the Register of
      Consents where the signer is a member, officer, employee, or contractor.
- [ ] **The registration plan is decided** — whether this work will be registered
      with the Copyright Office, by when, and in whose name.

## The assignment

```

      [OFFICE]] (the "Assignee").

      Work is a work made for hire].

  C.  The Assignee wishes to acquire, and the Assignor wishes to
      transfer, all right, title, and interest in the copyright in the
      Works, so that the Assignee may register, license, publish, and
      enforce them.

  D.  This Assignment is made in writing and signed by the Assignor in
      order to satisfy 17 U.S.C. § 204(a).

THE PARTIES AGREE:


1.  ASSIGNMENT

1.1 In consideration of the sum of [$1.00 / $[AMOUNT]] paid by the
    Assignee to the Assignor, receipt of which the Assignor acknowledges,

    undertaking in clause 4.1 to attribute the Work to the Assignor"],
    the Assignor hereby irrevocably assigns, transfers, and conveys to
    the Assignee, absolutely and throughout the world:

    (a) all right, title, and interest in and to the copyright in each

        reproduce the Work, to prepare derivative works based upon it, to
        distribute copies, to perform it publicly, to display it

        publicly by means of a digital audio transmission;

    (b) all such rights for the full term of copyright in each Work and
        for all renewals, extensions, revivals, and restorations of that
        term, in the United States and in every other country;

    (c) all rights to register the copyright in each Work in the name of
        the Assignee, and to record this Assignment, with the United
        States Copyright Office and with any corresponding authority in
        any other country;

    (d) all claims and causes of action for infringement of the copyright
        in each Work, whether arising before, on, or after the date of
        this Assignment, together with the right to sue for and to
        recover and retain all damages, profits, and other relief in
        respect of any such infringement, including infringement occurring
        before the date of this Assignment; and

    (e) all rights of action, remedies, and other benefits accruing to
        the owner of the copyright in each Work.

1.2 This Assignment takes effect on the date first written above.
    [WHERE THE WORKS WERE CREATED EARLIER AND THE PARTIES SO INTEND: The
    Parties confirm that the Assignor and the Assignee agreed to this
    transfer orally on [DATE], and this instrument records and confirms
    that agreement in writing.]

1.3 Nothing in this Assignment transfers ownership of any physical object
    in which a Work is embodied. Transfer of any such object is dealt
    with separately and, as 17 U.S.C. § 202 provides, carries no
    copyright with it.


2.  WORKS OF VISUAL ART

[INCLUDE THIS ARTICLE ONLY WHERE A WORK IS A WORK OF VISUAL ART WITHIN
17 U.S.C. § 101 — A PAINTING, DRAWING, PRINT, SCULPTURE, OR SIGNED
LIMITED-EDITION PHOTOGRAPH. DELETE OTHERWISE.]

2.1 The Assignor acknowledges that the rights of attribution and
    integrity conferred by 17 U.S.C. § 106A are personal to the author
    and are not transferred by this Assignment.

2.2 The Assignor expressly and irrevocably waives those rights in respect
    of the following Work, specifically identified: [TITLE AND
    DESCRIPTION OF THE WORK], and in respect of the following uses of
    that Work: [SPECIFY THE USES — e.g., "reproduction in any medium at
    any size; incorporation into letterhead, signage, publications,
    digital media, and merchandise; recolouring, cropping, and adaptation
    for those purposes; and display in any location"].

2.3 The waiver in clause 2.2 extends to no Work and no use other than
    those it identifies.


3.  ASSIGNOR'S WARRANTIES

The Assignor represents and warrants to the Assignee that:

3.1 the Assignor is the sole author of each Work and created it as an
    original work of authorship;

3.2 immediately before this Assignment the Assignor was the sole owner of
    all copyright in each Work, free of any lien, charge, licence,
    option, or other encumbrance;

3.3 the Assignor has not previously assigned, licensed, pledged, or
    otherwise disposed of any right in any Work to any person, and has
    not made any Work available under any public licence;

3.4 no Work was created within the scope of employment by any person
    other than [the Assignee / no person], and no Work is subject to any
    agreement designating it a work made for hire for any person other
    than the Assignee;

3.5 so far as the Assignor is aware, no Work infringes the copyright,
    trademark, or other right of any person, and no claim to that effect
    has been made or threatened;

3.6 each Work is either wholly original to the Assignor or, to the extent
    it incorporates material created by another person, that material is
    identified in Schedule A together with the licence or permission
    under which it is used; and

3.7 the Assignor has full capacity and authority to enter into this
    Assignment.


4.  ATTRIBUTION AND MORAL CONSIDERATIONS

4.1 [OPTIONAL — WHERE THE KINGDOM IS WILLING TO GIVE IT: The Assignee
    will credit the Assignor as author of each Work in the form "[FORM OF
    CREDIT]" wherever the Assignee publishes the Work in a context in
    which authorship is customarily credited. This undertaking is
    personal to the Assignor, is not a condition of the Assignment, and
    a failure to give credit does not affect the transfer made by
    clause 1.1.]


5.  FURTHER ASSURANCES

5.1 The Assignor will, at the Assignee's reasonable request and at the
    Assignee's expense, promptly execute any further document and do any
    further act that the Assignee reasonably requires in order to
    perfect, register, record, or enforce the rights assigned — including
    signing applications to register copyright, declarations in support
    of registration, documents for recordation under 17 U.S.C. § 205, and
    any document required in connection with proceedings against an
    infringer.

5.2 The Assignor will provide the Assignee with the best available copy
    or master of each Work, together with any source file, working file,
    or original, and will cooperate in identifying the date of creation
    and of first publication.

5.3 The obligations in this Article 5 continue after the date of this
    Assignment.


6.  GENERAL

6.1 This Assignment is governed by the law of the State of Connecticut,
    save that questions of copyright ownership, subsistence, and
    infringement are governed by the Copyright Act of 1976, 17 U.S.C.
    § 101 et seq.

6.2 If any provision is held invalid or unenforceable, it is severed and
    the remainder continues in force.

6.3 This Assignment is the entire agreement between the Parties on its
    subject matter and may be amended only in a writing signed by both.

6.4 This Assignment may be executed in counterparts, each of which is an
    original and all of which together constitute one instrument.

6.5 The Assignee will deliver an executed copy of this Assignment to the
    Assignor.
```

## Notes

**Why an oral transfer is void.** 17 U.S.C. § 204(a) provides that a transfer of
copyright ownership, other than by operation of law, is not valid unless an
instrument of conveyance, or a note or memorandum of the transfer, is in writing
and signed by the owner of the rights conveyed or that owner's duly authorised
agent. There is no informal route around it. A member who says "of course the
Kingdom owns it" has said something with no legal effect whatever, and so has an
email thread, a meeting minute, and thirty years of everyone assuming it.

The provision is forgiving in one narrow respect and it is not a plan. Where the
parties genuinely did agree orally, a later signed writing can memorialise the
earlier transfer — a court has enforced a one-line writing between the two parties
to it (*Effects Associates, Inc. v. Cohen*, 908 F.2d 555 (9th Cir. 1990)) — which
is what clause 1.2's bracketed sentence is for. But that doctrine protects the
parties from each other. It does not help when the author is unavailable, has
died, has changed their mind, or has been approached by the person the Kingdom is
suing. Get the writing.

Note also what does *not* require a writing: a non-exclusive licence. A volunteer
who hands over artwork and says use it has probably given the Kingdom an implied
non-exclusive licence, which is enough to use the work and nowhere near enough to
register it, to stop someone else from using it, or to sue. Only the owner of an
exclusive right may bring an infringement action (17 U.S.C. § 501(b)).

**Why "work made for hire" cannot be recited into existence for a volunteer.**
The statutory definition in 17 U.S.C. § 101 has two branches and no third. Either
the work was prepared by an *employee* within the scope of employment, or it was
specially ordered or commissioned for use in one of nine enumerated categories —
a contribution to a collective work, part of a motion picture or other
audiovisual work, a translation, a supplementary work, a compilation, an
instructional text, a test, answer material for a test, or an atlas — *and* the
parties expressly agreed in a signed written instrument that it is a work made for
hire.

Whether someone is an employee is decided on the common-law agency factors, not on
what the document calls them: the hiring party's right to control the manner and
means of the work, the skill required, who provides the tools and the workspace,
the duration of the relationship, whether the hiring party can assign additional
projects, the method of payment, whether the work is part of the hiring party's
regular business, whether employee benefits are provided, and the tax treatment of
the worker (*Community for Creative Non-Violence v. Reid*, 490 U.S. 730 (1989)).
A volunteer who receives no pay, no benefits, no W-2, works their own hours with
their own equipment, and is thanked rather than supervised is not an employee, and
a recital saying otherwise does not make them one. Nor does the ordinary volunteer
work — a seal, a hymn, a photograph, a sermon series — fall into the nine
commissioned categories.

The failure mode is what makes this worth labouring. An institution that relies on
a work-made-for-hire recital and nothing else owns *nothing* if the recital fails,
because there is no assignment underneath it to fall back on. The template
therefore assigns outright in clause 1.1 and treats the employment question as a
matter of accurate recital in Recital B, belt and braces. Where a work genuinely
was made by an employee within the scope of employment, take the assignment
anyway. It costs a signature and removes the argument.

**Every work, including the Founder's — especially the Founder's.** Article IV of
the Charter frames the Kingdom's holdings as trust property held for the benefit
of members rather than as the Founder's personal assets. That framing is correct
and consequential, and it has to be made true by instruments rather than asserted.
Until the Founder executes an assignment, the copyright in the Charter text, the
seal, the liturgy, and the teaching materials sits in the Founder personally,
which means: the Kingdom cannot register those works in its own name without
misstating ownership; the Kingdom cannot sue an infringer, because it is not the
owner of an exclusive right; the works are exposed to the Founder's personal
creditors and pass through the Founder's estate rather than the trust; and the
Kingdom's own account of itself as a trust holding property in common is
contradicted by its most valuable assets.

The remedy is a morning's work, one Schedule A, and a notary.

**Do not structure this for a tax deduction.** An author who donates a copyright
in their own work generally gets a deduction limited to their basis in it, which
for a self-created work is usually close to nothing, because a self-created
literary, musical, or artistic work is not a capital asset in the author's hands
(26 U.S.C. § 1221(a)(3)) and 26 U.S.C. § 170(e)(1)(A) reduces the deduction
accordingly. Any deduction over $5,000 would also require a qualified appraisal.
Take the assignment for a nominal, actually-paid consideration and be done. Do not
issue a contribution acknowledgment stating a value; the Kingdom never values a
non-cash gift, and here there is nothing worth valuing.

**The termination right cannot be waived, and that is fine.** Under 17 U.S.C.
§ 203 an author who has granted a transfer of copyright executed on or after
1 January 1978 may terminate that grant during a five-year window beginning
thirty-five years after execution — or, where the grant covers the right of
publication, thirty-five years from publication or forty years from execution,
whichever ends earlier — on advance written notice served not less than two nor
more than ten years before the effective date. The statute provides that the right
exists notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary. So a clause purporting to
waive it is void, and its only effect is to tell a reader that the instrument was
drafted by someone who had not read the statute.

Two practical points follow. Termination does not apply to works made for hire.
And thirty-five years is a very long time in the life of an institution — long
enough that the right is a matter for the Kingdom's successors to diarise, not a
reason to hesitate now. Record the execution date in the Intellectual Property
Portfolio, which is where a successor will look.

**Record the assignment with the Copyright Office.** Recordation under 17 U.S.C.
§ 205 is optional but cheap, and it gives constructive notice of the transfer and
governs priority between conflicting transfers of the same rights. Where the
Kingdom is about to register or enforce a work that came to it by assignment, the
recorded assignment is also the document that answers the chain-of-title question
before opposing counsel has finished asking it.

**Then register the work.** The assignment establishes ownership; registration is
what makes ownership worth something. No infringement suit over a United States
work may be instituted until the Copyright Office has acted on the application
(17 U.S.C. § 411(a); *Fourth Estate Publishing Ass'n v. Wall-Street.com, LLC*, 586
U.S. 296 (2019)), and under § 412 statutory damages and attorney's fees are
unavailable where registration came after the infringement began and more than
three months after first publication. That single rule decides whether an
infringement is worth pursuing at all. The Intellectual Property Portfolio raises
the alarm at day 75 for a reason.

**What this instrument is not.** It is a private conveyance between two parties,
made under a federal statute that requires nothing of anyone else. It is not
recorded against any person's property, it binds no one who has not signed it, and
it asserts nothing about the Kingdom's status. Keep it in that register.

---

*This is an operating template prepared to organise the Kingdom's affairs. It is
not legal advice and no attorney-client relationship arises from it. Chain of
title, entity capacity to hold property, and the treatment of works created by
volunteers and contractors turn on specific facts. Engage licensed Connecticut
counsel before acting on any of it, and take advice from counsel experienced in
copyright before any registration is filed in the Kingdom's name.*
